questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) State and explain the trend in the hydration energies of the group II sulphates down the group

(ii) Write an equation for the reaction of Barium with water

(iii) Would the reaction in a (ii) occur more vigorously or less vigorously than the reaction of Calcium with water? Explain

(iv) At a given high temperature, which of the two carbonates, Barium carbonate or Calcium carbonate, would decompose more easily? *[6 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Trend.** The **hydration energy (enthalpy of hydration) becomes less exothermic (smaller in magnitude) down the group** from Mg to Ba. Down the group the **ionic radius of $\mathrm{M^{2+}}$ increases** while the charge stays $2+$, so the **charge density falls** and the attraction between the cation and the polar $\mathrm{H_2O}$ molecules (ion-dipole interaction) becomes weaker, so less energy is released on hydration.

Consequence for the sulphates: the large $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$ ion makes the lattice enthalpy change only slightly with the cation size, whereas the hydration enthalpy decreases more markedly. The enthalpy of solution becomes less exothermic (more positive), so **the solubility of the sulphates decreases down the group**: $\mathrm{MgSO_4}$ is very soluble, $\mathrm{CaSO_4}$ slightly soluble, $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$ insoluble.

**(ii) Barium and water:**

$\mathrm{Ba} + 2\mathrm{H_2O} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ba(OH)_2} + \mathrm{H_2}$

(barium hydroxide solution and hydrogen gas).

**(iii) More vigorous.** Barium reacts **more vigorously** than calcium. Down the group the atoms are larger, so the two outer $s$ electrons are **further from the nucleus and better shielded**: the first and second ionisation energies decrease, and barium loses its electrons (forms $\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}$) more readily. Barium is more electropositive, hence a stronger reducing agent, so it reacts faster with water.

**(iv) Calcium carbonate decomposes more easily** (at a lower temperature). The small $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ ion has a **higher charge density (greater polarising power)** than the large $\mathrm{Ba^{2+}}$ ion, so it distorts the electron cloud of the carbonate ion more, weakening a C-O bond and making the formation of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and the oxide easier. Thermal stability of the Group II carbonates therefore increases down the group:

$\mathrm{CaCO_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO_2}$  (occurs at about $900^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$; $\mathrm{BaCO_3}$ needs a much higher temperature).

questions.enonce_markdown:
The Group IV (14) elements: Carbon (C), Silicon (Si), Germanium (Ge), Tin (Sn) and Lead (Pb), have melting points $3730^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, $1410^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, $937^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, $232^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and $327^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ respectively.

(i) Give the trend in the structure of the elements

(ii) Explain the variation in the melting points

(iii) Account for the fact that carbon tetrachloride is a insoluble in water. *[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Trend in structure.** Down the group the structure changes from **giant covalent (macromolecular)** to **giant metallic**: carbon (diamond), silicon and germanium have a giant covalent lattice in which each atom is covalently bonded to four others (diamond structure), whereas tin and lead have **giant metallic lattices** (positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons). Metallic character increases down the group.

**(ii) Variation in melting points.** The melting points fall sharply from C ($3730^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) to Sn ($232^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$):

- Melting a giant covalent solid means **breaking strong covalent bonds** throughout the lattice: C-C is very strong, so carbon has the highest melting point.
- Down the group the atoms get **larger**, bonding orbitals overlap less well, and the covalent bonds become **longer and weaker** (C-C > Si-Si > Ge-Ge), so less energy is needed: the melting point falls from C to Ge.
- Tin and lead are **metals**, held by **metallic bonding** which is weaker than the covalent bonding of C, Si and Ge, because the delocalised electrons are spread over large atoms; their melting points are low.
- Lead ($327^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) melts slightly higher than tin ($232^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$): an exception to the downward trend, attributed to the different metallic structures and bonding (Pb is more closely packed, with stronger metallic bonding than Sn).

**(iii) $\mathrm{CCl_4}$ is insoluble in water.** $\mathrm{CCl_4}$ is a **non-polar** molecule: it is tetrahedral and symmetrical, so the dipoles of the four polar C-Cl bonds cancel. It can form only weak instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (van der Waals) forces with water, which cannot compensate for the energy needed to break the strong **hydrogen bonds** between water molecules, and it cannot form hydrogen bonds itself. Hence it does not dissolve (like dissolves like). It also does not hydrolyse, because carbon has no low-energy vacant orbitals to accept a lone pair from water (unlike $\mathrm{SiCl_4}$).

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Complete the table below

| halogen | physical state | colour |
|---|---|---|
| Fluorine | | |
| Chlorine | | |
| Bromine | | |
| Iodine | | |

(ii) Write a balanced equation to show what happens when chlorine gas is bubbled into an aqueous solution of potassium bromide (KBr)

(iii) What are the observable changes?

(iv) An aqueous solution containing an unknown halide ion, was acidified with nitric acid; aqueous silver nitrate was then added. A cream precipitate was obtained which dissolves in concentrated aqueous ammonia. Identify the halide ion *[7 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Table.**

| Halogen | Physical state (at room temperature) | Colour |
|---|---|---|
| Fluorine | Gas | Pale yellow |
| Chlorine | Gas | Greenish-yellow |
| Bromine | Liquid (volatile, gives off vapour) | Red-brown (reddish-brown) |
| Iodine | Solid | Shiny grey-black (gives a violet vapour on warming) |

**(ii) Equation.** Chlorine is a stronger oxidising agent than bromine and displaces bromine from bromide:

$\mathrm{Cl_2} + 2\mathrm{KBr} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{KCl} + \mathrm{Br_2}$

(ionic form: $\mathrm{Cl_2} + 2\mathrm{Br^{-}} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cl^{-}} + \mathrm{Br_2}$)

**(iii) Observations.** The colourless potassium bromide solution turns **orange-brown (yellow-orange)** as bromine is formed, and the greenish-yellow colour of the chlorine gas disappears.

**(iv) Identity.** The nitric acid removes carbonate or hydroxide ions that would also give precipitates. A **cream precipitate** of silver bromide, $\mathrm{AgBr}$, forms:

$\mathrm{Ag^{+}} + \mathrm{Br^{-}} \rightarrow \mathrm{AgBr}$

and AgBr dissolves in **concentrated** ammonia (soluble in conc. but not in dilute) as the diamminesilver(I) complex. ($\mathrm{AgCl}$ is white and dissolves in dilute ammonia; $\mathrm{AgI}$ is pale yellow and does not dissolve even in concentrated ammonia.)

The halide ion is the **bromide ion, $\mathrm{Br^-}$.**
